items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: I went over to his house and he had these old Dial 78s. And he played them for me, and I said wow, I hadn’t heard anything like that.

ctx.x: I mean did you feel like you had too much, I don’t know how to put this, too much knowledge from your bebop playing?
That could be it. I felt like I was playing too much because you know, like when you get in the habit of playing like the modern changes, or as you say, bebop, it doesn’t fit with

what they’re doing. You’ve got to think one-three-five, you know what I’m saying? You don’t deviate from that one-three-five or one-four. And you stay in that bag all the time. You can’t play those slick changes like Charlie Parker was playing you know.

items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: like Charlie Parker worked there for a month, shoot one time I worked with Charlie Parker. He was one of the people that influenced me to come to New York.

ctx.x: Oh, I feel the same way. I was never a fast sight reader. But you know as a kid I learned how to read music but it’s something that, you have to keep doing it. Once you stop, you’re going to not do it as well. And I stopped for years, because I went to the small band type way of playing. My reading was probably best right after high school and my first year of Roosevelt College. I was with this local big band, the one I was talking about that Gene Ammons played in. It was like the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band of…

blues, maybe that’s something in the back of my mind as to why I don’t have that much music. I have some tunes you know. Occasionally I let them work on a bebop tune and let an ensemble do it, but other than that I just sort of got away from it. I was never that interested in getting back to it. I was never interested; and doing studio work, which is probably the most lucrative part of the business you know. Like look at the studio musicians now, even those into retirement, man they have pensions in five and six…
Did they ever bring their own library, or they just expected you to know —
